# Affect: states that last {#sec-affect}

<div data-life="status" data-stage="1.8"></div>

Everything this brain does so far, it does about the present. A bush is in front of it, so it bites. The skin is
cold, so it walks. The stomach is empty, so it forages. When the cause is gone, the behaviour is gone in the same
moment.

But some events say something about the minutes that follow. An animal that has just eaten well is probably
standing in a good place. An animal that has just been hurt is probably standing in a bad one. To use that, the
brain has to keep something of the event after it is over. This stage adds two such states: an alarm after pain,
and contentment after a meal. So that the states have something to work with, the bushes in this world grow in
patches that are mostly of one kind.

<div data-life="brain" data-stage="1.8"></div>

## The circuit

Two *modulators*, substances that a few cells release and that reach many cells at once, and three new cells.

- **Alarm.** Pain releases the modulator `alarm`. It drives a new cell, **`flee`**, which pushes the animal
  forward. After poison bites the animal keeps going for a while, out of the poisoned ground.
- **Serotonin.** A new cell, **`fed`**, fires when the animal tastes food, and releases the modulator `serotonin`.
  It drives a new cell, **`settle`**, which switches on `rest`, the cell of the previous stage that holds the
  forward step back. After a good meal the animal stays where it ate, also where it is cold.

`hungry` still shuts `rest`, as before. So a fed animal stays on good ground until it is hungry again, and then it
forages, with good bushes close by.

The two states are not a second system next to the drives. They act on the same cells: the drives decide what the
animal does from what the body needs now, and the two modulators push those same modes for a while after an event.

### States that build up

A modulator is released in small amounts and cleared slowly, so its level at any moment is a running sum of what
happened lately, not a record of the last event alone. The cells that read it fire only above a threshold. One
poison bite passes without alarm; the animal flees only when more than one comes within a short while. It settles
only after more good bites than one bush can give.

That matters in this world, where a patch is mostly one kind but not only one kind. A single bite says little about
the ground: a poison bush can stand in good ground, and a good bush in poor ground. Several bites close together
say much more.

The wiring and the thresholds are designed. Evolution may tune every strength, the thresholds, and how fast each
modulator is cleared, which sets how long each state lasts.

## The biology: affect

A drive, as in the previous stage, follows the body: the hunger cell fires for as long as the stomach is empty and
stops when it is full. An *affective state* is different in one respect. Something sets it off, and then it stays
for a while by itself, after its cause has gone.

In small animals such states are carried by *neuromodulators*. They are released quickly and cleared slowly, and
that slowness is the memory. The roundworm *C. elegans* slows down and stays where it is for minutes after it has
found food, under the influence of serotonin. After a harmful touch it speeds away, and keeps going well after
the touch has ended.

Such a state has two sides. It is good or bad, and it makes the animal more active or less. An animal that is
alarmed is in a bad and active state. An animal that is content is in a good and quiet one.

## The world: patches of mostly one kind

In the world of the previous stage the bushes of every kind were spread evenly. There, a meal says nothing about
the place: what grows next to the bush just emptied is as likely to be poison as anywhere else. A state that
lasts has nothing to work with.

So the bushes now grow in patches, and most bushes in a patch are of one kind. After good meals, the neighbouring
bushes are most likely good as well. After poison bites, the neighbours are most likely poison too.

Not every bush in a patch is of the patch's kind. In patches of only one kind, the first bite tells the animal all
it needs to know about the bushes around it, and knowing a poison by its look, the lesson of the association
stage, has nothing left to do. With other kinds standing among them, there is still a reason to know a bush by its
look.

The world is also larger than before, four times the area for the same number of animals, with more food. In the
smaller world the animals took food from each other, and the better they foraged the more they did, so that what a
better forager gains was mostly hidden. This is the world the next chapter starts in.

The rest is as before: the world is cold, the hot springs are spread evenly, and the four kinds of berry bush are
new in every life, half of them poison.

## Results

How to read the table and the charts: see [How a stage is judged](index.qmd#sec-judged).

### Main against control

The control is the brain of the previous stage in this world of patches. It feels pain and tastes food as before,
but nothing of either stays with it.

<div data-life="curves" data-stage="1.8"></div>

<div data-life="summary" data-stage="1.8"></div>

The animals with the two states come out ahead of the control in two seeds out of three. In the third the two
end about level: re-evaluated in the same worlds the control is somewhat ahead, and when both live in one world
together the main animals are slightly ahead. Over the three seeds the gain is clear when the two populations share
a world, and weaker when each lives among its own kind.

### Is the circuit used?

<div data-life="lesions" data-stage="1.8"></div>

The two states are used in every seed. Silencing `flee` costs the most of the new cells: the alarm now acts on a
run of poison bites, which in these mixed patches is the clearest sign of bad ground. `fed` and `settle` are two
links of one chain and cost about the same. `rest`, through which both staying after a meal and staying in the
warmth act, costs more than either.

Two things from earlier stages are not used in this world.

- Silencing `cold` or `warm_seek` costs nothing, as with the first version of this stage. A fed animal that walks
  off in search of warmth leaves the good ground, and staying where the food is turns out to be worth more.
- Switching the learning off costs nothing either. In these patches the look of a bush and the ground it stands on
  say much the same thing, and the animals lean on the ground: two poison bites in a row and the alarm carries
  them off. Learning is not lost, though. Its strength is still there in every seed, at about the level where a
  lesson stays on the food it was learned about. What keeps it from paying is that a lesson about one berry spreads
  to the berries that look like it. That is the problem the next chapter starts with.

Neither was removed. The cells belong to the previous stages as they were frozen, and the next stages need the
learning.

### After a bite

<div data-life="table" data-stage="1.8" data-example="after_a_bite"></div>

After poison bites the animals of this stage take a few more steps than the control, and after a good meal a
little fewer. The differences are small in this measure, because one bite alone no longer sets a state off: it
takes several.

### How a life is spent

<div data-life="table" data-stage="1.8" data-example="life_spent"></div>

Both populations stand still for most of their life. Much of that time they bite at nothing: an animal held in
place by `rest` still has its grasp programme, and a bite costs little.
